title: Temporal dissipative solitons and optical frequency combs in coherently driven Kerr resonators
authors: Stuart G. Murdoch, François Leo, Xiaoxiao Xue, Stéphane Coen, Miro Erkintalo
abstract: Kerr frequency combs have recently emerged as an exciting new photonic technology, with applications across science and engineering. Their formation within driven optical resonators that possess a Kerr nonlinearity is enabled through the rich landscape of localized nonlinear dissipative structures intrinsic to these systems. This article offers a comprehensive review of the physics that underpins these nonlinear comb-generating structures. Particular attention is placed on bright temporal cavity solitons and nonlinear switching waves -- the canonical stable comb-generating states in the anomalous and normal dispersion regimes, respectively. Written as both a review and tutorial, the article also includes an in-depth treatment of the numerical methods required to simulate driven Kerr resonators, alongside a comprehensive discussion of the laboratory techniques used to experimentally realize and characterize Kerr combs.
summary: This comprehensive review details the physics behind generating optical frequency combs using Kerr resonators. It explains that these combs arise from localized nonlinear dissipative structures like temporal solitons, which stabilize the system's output despite losses. The paper integrates advanced theoretical modeling with practical experimental techniques used in modern integrated photonics.
main_problem: The article reviews the fundamental physics governing Kerr frequency combs generated by localized nonlinear dissipative structures within coherently driven optical resonators.
main_result: It details how bright temporal cavity solitons (in anomalous dispersion) and nonlinear switching waves (in normal dispersion) act as canonical stable states enabling robust, coherent comb generation in microresonators.
method: The review synthesizes theoretical modeling using the Generalized Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation (GNLSE), coupled with discrete map approaches (Ikeda map), alongside comprehensive discussions of experimental characterization techniques.
model_or_system: The primary system is a Kerr nonlinear optical resonator, modeled by equations describing intracavity field evolution over multiple passes. Platforms range from long optical fibers to integrated monolithic microresonators (e.g., MgF2).
key_observables: Temporal and spectral intensity profiles of the intracavity field; cavity power enhancement factor; frequency spacing (FSR); stability metrics like timing jitter.
important_parameters: Dispersion regime (anomalous vs. normal GVD), Kerr nonlinearity ($\gamma$), resonator loss ($\alpha$), and coupling strength ($	heta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on the mean-field approximation for high-finesse cavities, assuming point coupling losses and single-mode operation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate linear resonance behavior (Fabry-Perot), nonlinear resonance shifts due to Kerr effects, and comparisons between predictions from the Ikeda map versus simplified mean-field models.
paper_structure: The article is structured as a comprehensive review/tutorial, covering modeling dispersive resonators, dedicated sections for temporal cavity solitons (anomalous regime), localized structures in normal dispersion (switching waves), and experimental realization techniques.
why_interesting: This work bridges nonlinear wave physics with applied quantum optics by studying dissipative, non-Hamiltonian systems. The concepts of stable attractors (solitons) in driven, lossy environments are highly relevant to open quantum system dynamics and cavity QED modeling.
